title: The sermon he didn't give
hook: "do you know what I'll say?" and whatever the crowd answers, he finds a reason not to preach (Nasruddin tale)
carry: let those who know tell the others

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pot that gave birth, and then died. Your line was if it can give birth. Which pleasant little story did you check twice? Day forty-one.

A speaker clears his throat and says, I'll be brief. Forty minutes later, the back row is counting ceiling tiles. Nasruddin's sermon goes wrong the other way. The village has asked Nasruddin to give the sermon. The room fills up. People have come to hear the famous teacher. He climbs up, looks out at all of them, and asks a single question: do you know what I'm going to say? And whatever they answer, he finds a way not to say it. Three weeks in a row. Today's story is the sermon he didn't give.
screen: `I'LL BE BRIEF.` → `THE ROOM FILLS UP.` → `DO YOU KNOW WHAT I'LL SAY?`

segments.voice: The first week, the crowd answers honestly: no, we don't know. And Nasruddin says: then I have nothing to say to people who don't even know what I'm talking about. And he climbs down and goes home. The next week, they've worked it out. Do you know what I'm going to say? Yes! they shout. Then, says Nasruddin, there's no need for me to tell you. And he goes home again. The third week, they've made a plan. When he asks, half the room shouts yes and half shouts no. Surely now he has to preach. Nasruddin smiles. Wonderful, he says. Let those who know tell those who don't. And he goes home. It's a trickster's escape, three times, and it's funny because he wriggles out of work every single week. But the last line is better than a joke. Let those who know tell the others. The crowd came to receive wisdom from one man at the front. Nasruddin hands the job back to them. Half the room already knows something. The other half needs it. They don't need him standing between them. A lot of learning happens that way: not from the pulpit, but from the person in the next seat who figured it out last week. A grandmother showing how to fold the dough. A coworker who knows the shortcut. A friend who went through it first. Each of us is on the knowing side of something. So the question the story leaves is not what Nasruddin would have said. It's what you know that someone near you doesn't, yet.
screen: `NO? THEN I HAVE NOTHING TO SAY.` · `YES? THEN NO NEED TO TELL YOU.` · `HALF KNOW, HALF DON'T.` · `THE JOB GOES BACK TO THE ROOM.` · then, large: `LET THOSE WHO KNOW TELL THE OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: teach someone one small thing. For now, settle, and breathe, and find it. What do you know that someone near you doesn't? A recipe. A shortcut on the phone. The name of a bird. How to say sorry to your aunt so she actually hears it. Something you learned on this path. Pick one small thing, and pick one person you could give it to today. Picture handing it over, simply, no sermon. The bell holds the time.
The sermon he didn't give. Three weeks, three escapes, and a last line that hands the teaching back to the room. Today's word.
screen: `THE SERMON HE DIDN'T GIVE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: let those who know tell the others. Today, be one of those who know. Teach one person one small thing, in under a minute. Day forty-one.

howItsDone: The unpreached sermon is a Nasruddin tale told in Turkey, Iran, Central Asia and beyond, and its last line is sometimes borrowed by teachers who want a class to teach each other.

original.note: Arabic, khutba: a sermon, like the one given at Friday prayers. Tellings differ on which kind of sermon Nasruddin was asked to give.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lazy teacher dodging work.
what it means: people who know something can teach those who don't, without anyone at the front.
what a scholar hears: a three-part trickster tale, the classic folk rhythm of three tries, ending on a line that turns the escape into the lesson.

notes: Tellings vary on the setting (a mosque, a village gathering) and on the kind of sermon; the script keeps it general ('the village has asked Nasruddin to give the sermon').
Arabic خطبة (khutba) as the original-language word: confirm it fits, since Turkish tellings may use vaaz for a general sermon.
The joke's 'nothing to say to people who don't even know what I'm talking about' is a paraphrase of the common telling.
